questions.stem: The ideological rivalry at the heart of the Cold War was between:
options: constitutional monarchy in the USA and absolute monarchy in the Soviet Union
Christian democracy in the USA and Islamic republicanism in the Soviet Union
liberal capitalism in the USA and Marxist-Leninist communism in the USSR
fascism in the USA and liberal democracy in the Soviet Union and its allies
questions.explanation: The USA promoted free markets, private property and multiparty democracy; the USSR promoted a one-party state, a planned economy and the eventual triumph of communism. Each saw the other's system as a threat to its own.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how ideology and security combined to shape Soviet policy in Eastern Europe after 1945?
options: Stalin wanted to spread democracy to Eastern Europe so the region could join the Marshall Plan with Soviet approval
Stalin wanted to withdraw from Eastern Europe as soon as possible and let the United Nations govern the region
Stalin wanted to restore the pre-war governments of Eastern Europe to win the trust of Britain and the USA
Stalin wanted a buffer of friendly states against invasion from the west, and communist rule seemed the surest guarantee
questions.explanation: The USSR had been invaded through Poland twice in thirty years and lost many millions of people in the Second World War. Stalin saw communist governments loyal to Moscow as the most reliable way to secure the region, while Marxist ideology predicted conflict with capitalism.

questions.stem: George Kennan's 'Long Telegram' of February 1946 influenced US policy by arguing that the Soviet Union:
options: should be attacked at once with atomic weapons while the USA still had a monopoly
was expansionist but cautious, and could be contained by firm, long-term resistance
was a peaceful, satisfied state that wanted only friendship and trade with the Western powers
was about to collapse, so the USA should simply wait for the regime to fall apart
questions.explanation: Kennan, a diplomat in Moscow, argued that Soviet insecurity and ideology drove expansion, but that the USSR would retreat when met with strength. His analysis became the basis of containment.

questions.stem: In March 1947 the Truman Doctrine committed the USA to:
options: support free peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures
withdraw all American troops from Europe and return to a policy of isolation
share the secrets of the atomic bomb with the Soviet Union through the UN
rebuild the German economy as a neutral state outside any military alliance
questions.explanation: Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey and set out a general commitment to resist the spread of communism. It marked a break from isolationism and the start of containment as public policy.

questions.stem: Why did the USA see the Marshall Plan, announced in 1947, as part of containment?
options: It paid Eastern European governments to leave the Soviet bloc and join a military alliance
It was a loan to the USSR that Stalin could repay only by withdrawing from Eastern Europe
Economic recovery would reduce the poverty and despair that helped communist parties win support
It required every country receiving aid to station Soviet troops on its territory as a guarantee
questions.explanation: The European Recovery Program provided billions of dollars to rebuild Western Europe, where communist parties were strong in countries such as France and Italy. Stalin refused aid for the USSR and forbade Eastern European states to accept it.

questions.stem: The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), founded in April 1949, was based on the principle that:
options: an armed attack on one member would be considered an attack on them all
each member would give up its own army and join a single European force
members would trade only with each other and not with communist states
the USA would govern the defence of Western Europe from its base in Berlin
questions.explanation: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty made collective defence the core of the alliance, binding the USA to Western Europe's security for the first time in peacetime. Members kept their own armed forces.

questions.stem: President Eisenhower's 'domino theory' of 1954 was used mainly to justify US involvement in:
options: Western Europe, especially in rebuilding West Germany's armed forces
Latin America, especially in the invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs
the Middle East, especially in supporting Britain and France during the Suez Crisis
South-East Asia, especially in supporting South Vietnam against communism
questions.explanation: Eisenhower argued that if Indochina fell to communism, neighbouring states would fall in turn. The theory underpinned US support for South Vietnam and the formation of SEATO in 1954. The USA opposed Britain at Suez in 1956.

questions.stem: NSC-68, a US policy paper of 1950, changed containment mainly by:
options: calling for an end to military spending and a return to economic aid only
calling for a negotiated withdrawal of US forces from Europe and Japan
calling for an immediate pre-emptive war against the Soviet Union and China
calling for a large military build-up to meet the Soviet threat everywhere
questions.explanation: After the Soviet atomic test and the communist victory in China in 1949, NSC-68 argued that the USA must greatly increase defence spending. The Korean War, which began in June 1950, led Truman to adopt its recommendations.

questions.stem: Which development of 1948 shows Soviet intervention in Eastern Europe?
options: a communist takeover in Czechoslovakia that ended its multiparty government
a Soviet withdrawal from Poland that allowed free multiparty elections the next year
a Soviet agreement for Austria to join NATO in return for war reparations
an alliance with Yugoslavia that made Tito the leader of the Cominform
questions.explanation: In February 1948 the Czechoslovak communists, backed by Moscow, forced the non-communist ministers out and took full control. In the same year Tito's Yugoslavia was expelled from the Cominform for defying Stalin.

questions.stem: The Warsaw Pact of May 1955 was:
options: an agreement banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere and outer space
a military alliance of the USSR and its Eastern European satellite states
a trade agreement between the USSR and the members of the Marshall Plan
a treaty ending the occupation of Germany and allowing its immediate reunification
questions.explanation: The pact was signed days after West Germany joined NATO and gave the USSR a formal military command over its satellites. It was later used to justify the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

questions.stem: Khrushchev's policy of 'peaceful coexistence', announced in 1956, meant that:
options: war between the two systems was not inevitable, and competition could be economic and political
the Soviet Union would abandon communism and join the Western alliance within ten years
the Soviet Union would allow its Eastern European satellites to leave the Warsaw Pact freely
the two superpowers would merge their economies under the authority of the United Nations
questions.explanation: At the Twentieth Party Congress Khrushchev argued that nuclear war would be catastrophic and that communism could triumph through peaceful competition. It did not mean freedom for the satellites, as Hungary found in 1956.

questions.stem: The Soviet crushing of the Hungarian uprising in 1956 and the Prague Spring in 1968 shows that peaceful coexistence:
options: did not extend to letting the satellite states leave Soviet control
required the USSR to consult NATO before using force in Eastern Europe
meant that the USA had agreed to defend Hungary and Czechoslovakia
was abandoned completely by the USSR in favour of world revolution
questions.explanation: Moscow tolerated reform only within limits; Hungary's attempt to leave the Warsaw Pact and Czechoslovakia's liberalisation brought invasions. The West protested but did not intervene, implicitly accepting a Soviet sphere.

questions.stem: The Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948-1949 was defeated by:
options: a United Nations vote that ordered the Soviet Union to end the blockade
a secret agreement giving East Germany control of the western sectors
a Western airlift that supplied the city by air for almost a year
a Western land invasion that broke through the Soviet checkpoints
questions.explanation: American, British and other aircraft flew in food, coal and other supplies until Stalin lifted the blockade in May 1949. Using the air corridors avoided a direct armed clash on the ground.

questions.stem: Which was the most important long-term impact of the Berlin Blockade?
options: It led the USA to withdraw from Berlin and leave the city to the Soviet Union
It ended the occupation of Germany and the presence of all foreign troops
It hastened the division of Germany into two states and the creation of NATO
It united Germany as a neutral state with its capital in Berlin from 1949
questions.explanation: In 1949 the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic were founded, and the blockade convinced Western governments to form NATO. Germany remained divided and occupied until 1990.

questions.stem: East Germany built the Berlin Wall in August 1961 mainly to:
options: protect East Berlin from an imminent invasion by American and British forces based in West Germany
mark the border agreed with the Western powers in a new treaty signed that year
keep West Berliners from crossing to the East to buy cheaper goods and services
stop the flow of its citizens, especially skilled workers, to the West through Berlin
questions.explanation: Millions had left the GDR, many through the open border in Berlin, draining it of professionals and workers. The official claim that the Wall was an 'anti-fascist protection rampart' was propaganda.

questions.stem: How did the building of the Berlin Wall affect Cold War tensions in the longer term?
options: It became a symbol of division, yet it stabilised the Berlin question by ending the refugee crisis
It led directly to war between NATO and the Warsaw Pact in Berlin in the autumn of 1961
It persuaded the USSR to hand East Berlin to the Western powers in return for recognition
It ended the arms race because both sides agreed that the Wall made war in Europe impossible
questions.explanation: The Wall became the great symbol of communist repression, but by sealing the border it removed the issue that had prompted Khrushchev's ultimatums since 1958. A tense tank stand-off at Checkpoint Charlie in October 1961 ended without fighting.

questions.stem: Which was a cause of the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962?
options: The USA had placed nuclear missiles in Cuba and the USSR demanded their removal
The UN had asked the USSR to station missiles in Cuba to keep peace in the region
Khrushchev wanted to protect Castro's Cuba and offset American missiles near the USSR
Castro wanted to invade Florida and asked the USSR for troops and ships to support the attack
questions.explanation: After the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961, Khrushchev sent missiles to deter another US attack on Cuba and to reduce the USA's lead in long-range missiles, including Jupiter missiles in Turkey. US spy planes photographed the sites in October 1962.

questions.stem: President Kennedy's response to the discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba was to:
options: announce a naval 'quarantine' to stop further Soviet weapons reaching Cuba
order an immediate air strike and invasion to remove the missile sites
withdraw American forces from West Berlin in exchange for removing the missiles
ask Castro to remove the missiles in return for American economic aid
questions.explanation: On 22 October 1962 Kennedy announced a blockade, called a quarantine, and demanded the missiles' removal, while keeping air strikes as an option. An invasion was considered but rejected as too risky.

questions.stem: Which was an impact of the Cuban Missile Crisis on superpower relations?
options: Castro was removed from power and Cuba rejoined the Organisation of American States
A direct hotline was set up and the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in 1963
The USSR left the United Nations and refused to talk to the USA for a decade
The USA and USSR agreed to abolish all nuclear weapons by the end of the 1960s
questions.explanation: Having come close to nuclear war, both sides created the Moscow-Washington hotline and banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water. But the USSR also resolved never again to be outgunned and expanded its arsenal.

questions.stem: The Soviet Union ended the American monopoly on atomic weapons with its first test in:
questions.explanation: The USSR tested its first atomic bomb in August 1949, years earlier than many in the West had expected, helped by espionage. The USA had used atomic bombs in 1945, and Sputnik was launched in 1957.

questions.stem: Why did the Soviet launch of Sputnik in October 1957 intensify the arms race as well as the space race?
options: The launch revealed that the USA had already landed astronauts on the Moon in secret
Sputnik was launched from Cuba, which proved that the USSR had bases near the USA
The rocket that launched it showed the USSR could reach the USA with an intercontinental missile
Sputnik carried a nuclear weapon that orbited over the USA for several months before landing
questions.explanation: Sputnik was launched by an R-7 rocket, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile. Americans feared a 'missile gap', and the USA set up NASA in 1958 and expanded science education and missile programs.

questions.stem: Who became the first person to travel into space, in April 1961?
options: Alan Shepard
Neil Armstrong
John Glenn
Yuri Gagarin
questions.explanation: Gagarin orbited the Earth on 12 April 1961, a major propaganda victory for the USSR. Shepard made a suborbital flight in May 1961, Glenn was the first American to orbit in 1962, and Armstrong walked on the Moon in 1969.

questions.stem: Mutually assured destruction (MAD) was thought to keep the peace because:
options: each side had agreed to destroy its own weapons if the other side attacked first
each side had built shelters that would protect its whole population from attack
each side allowed the United Nations to control the launch codes of all its nuclear missiles
each side could survive a first strike and still destroy the other, so neither would attack
questions.explanation: Because a surviving 'second-strike' force could devastate any attacker, starting a nuclear war would be suicidal. This logic encouraged both sides to build secure forces such as submarine-launched missiles.

questions.stem: Which was a reason for detente in the late 1960s and 1970s?
options: the collapse of communism in the Soviet Union and the end of the Warsaw Pact
an agreement by the USSR to allow free elections throughout Eastern Europe
the unification of Germany, which removed the main cause of tension in Europe
rough nuclear parity, the cost of the arms race, and US weariness from the Vietnam War
questions.explanation: By the late 1960s the USSR had nearly matched US nuclear strength, both economies felt the burden of arms spending, and the USA was seeking to reduce its commitments after Vietnam. The other options describe events of 1989-1991.

questions.stem: The SALT I agreements signed in Moscow in 1972 included:
options: the complete abolition of intermediate-range nuclear missiles in Europe
a ban on all nuclear tests, including underground tests, by both sides
the withdrawal of all Soviet and American troops from Central Europe
the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and limits on numbers of strategic missiles
questions.explanation: Nixon and Brezhnev signed the ABM Treaty, limiting missile defences, and an interim agreement freezing numbers of launchers. The INF Treaty abolishing intermediate-range missiles came in 1987.

questions.stem: In the Helsinki Final Act of 1975, the Western states accepted Europe's post-war borders. In return the Soviet bloc:
options: agreed to leave the Warsaw Pact and join a neutral group of European states
promised to hold free elections in every Eastern European state by the end of 1976
promised to respect human rights, which dissidents then used to criticise their governments
agreed to withdraw from East Germany and allow Germany to reunite within the following five years
questions.explanation: The Soviet bloc gained recognition of the post-1945 borders, but its human rights commitments inspired monitoring groups such as Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia. Many historians see this as an unexpected long-term weakness for the communist regimes.

questions.stem: Which development best explains why detente had broken down by the end of the 1970s?
options: The Soviet decision to leave the United Nations Security Council after the Helsinki Final Act of 1975
Soviet involvement in Africa, new SS-20 missiles in Europe and the invasion of Afghanistan
The USA's refusal to sign any arms control agreement with the USSR during the 1970s
The reunification of Vietnam, which the USA and the USSR had both strongly opposed
questions.explanation: Soviet-backed interventions in Angola and Ethiopia, the deployment of SS-20s and human rights disputes eroded American support, and the invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 ended detente. The USA signed SALT I and SALT II, though SALT II was never ratified.

questions.stem: How did the Vietnam War contribute to detente?
options: It ended with a joint US-Soviet victory that brought the two superpowers into a lasting alliance
It persuaded the USSR to stop supplying North Vietnam, which pleased the American public
It forced China to join the Warsaw Pact, which made the USA seek peace with the USSR
It led the USA to seek to limit its overseas commitments and to improve relations with the USSR and China
questions.explanation: Under the Nixon Doctrine of 1969 the USA expected allies to provide their own troops, and Nixon hoped Moscow and Beijing would press Hanoi towards a settlement. The USSR and China both kept supplying North Vietnam.

questions.stem: Armed clashes between the Soviet Union and China along their border took place in:
questions.explanation: Fighting over Zhenbao (Damansky) Island on the Ussuri River in March 1969 showed how deep the Sino-Soviet split had become. In 1950 the two had signed a treaty of friendship.

questions.stem: Nixon's visit to China in February 1972 changed the Cold War mainly because it:
options: restored the Nationalist government of Taiwan to control of mainland China in that year
exploited the Sino-Soviet split, putting pressure on Moscow to improve relations with the USA
brought China into NATO, which isolated the Soviet Union in both Asia and Europe at the same time
ended the Vietnam War at once, because China agreed to stop the fighting in South Vietnam
questions.explanation: 'Triangular diplomacy' meant the USSR feared a US-China alignment, which encouraged it to sign SALT I in May 1972. The visit did not end the Vietnam War, which for the USA ended with the Paris Peace Accords of 1973.

questions.stem: How did the USA respond to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979?
options: It declared war on the Soviet Union and bombed Soviet bases in Central Asia in 1980
It halted grain sales, led a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics and aided the mujahideen
It sent American troops to fight alongside the Soviet army against the Afghan rebels
It ignored the invasion and signed a new long-term trade agreement with the Soviet Union in 1980
questions.explanation: Carter imposed a grain embargo, withdrew SALT II from the Senate, announced the Carter Doctrine to protect the Persian Gulf and led an Olympic boycott. The CIA, working with Pakistan, armed the Afghan resistance.

questions.stem: Why is the war in Afghanistan often called the Soviet Union's 'Vietnam'?
options: It was won quickly by the Soviet army, just as the USA had won quickly in Vietnam
It was a long, costly war against guerrillas that the USSR could not win and that hurt morale at home
It was fought against American troops, who drove the Soviet army out of Afghanistan in 1985
It ended with the division of Afghanistan into a communist north and a non-communist south
questions.explanation: Soviet forces fought for about nine years against mujahideen armed by the USA and others, suffered heavy losses and withdrew in February 1989. The war damaged the army's prestige and became a target of criticism under glasnost.

questions.stem: Which policy was part of Ronald Reagan's strategy towards the Soviet Union in the early 1980s?
options: an immediate withdrawal of US missiles from Western Europe to reassure the Soviet leadership
a large program of loans and grain sales to help the Soviet economy recover from stagnation
an agreement to recognise Soviet control of Afghanistan in return for arms reductions
a major military build-up, support for anti-communist rebels and the Strategic Defense Initiative
questions.explanation: Reagan raised defence spending, called the USSR an 'evil empire', supported insurgents in Afghanistan, Nicaragua and Angola (the Reagan Doctrine) and announced SDI in 1983. Pershing II and cruise missiles were deployed in Western Europe from 1983.

questions.stem: Historians debate Reagan's role in ending the Cold War. Which argument challenges the view that his pressure caused the Soviet collapse?
options: Soviet economic decline and Gorbachev's own choices mattered more than US military spending
Reagan reduced US defence spending to its lowest level since the Second World War
Reagan refused ever to meet Gorbachev, so his policies could not have affected Soviet decisions
The Soviet Union was growing faster than the USA in the 1980s, so pressure had no effect
questions.explanation: Critics of the 'triumphalist' view argue that the Soviet system was already stagnating and that Gorbachev chose reform and retreat. Reagan in fact raised defence spending and met Gorbachev at four summits from 1985.

questions.stem: Gorbachev's 'new thinking' in foreign policy included:
options: arms reduction, withdrawal from Afghanistan and abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine
a new military build-up, intervention in Poland and firm support for the Berlin Wall
an alliance with China against the USA and a return to Stalin's foreign policy
the deployment of SS-20 missiles in Cuba and the expansion of the Warsaw Pact
questions.explanation: Gorbachev believed the USSR could not afford confrontation. He signed the INF Treaty in 1987, announced unilateral troop cuts at the UN in 1988, withdrew from Afghanistan by 1989 and let Eastern Europe choose its own path.

questions.stem: The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty of 1987 was significant because it:
options: ended the Warsaw Pact and the Soviet occupation of East Germany
banned the testing of nuclear weapons in the atmosphere
eliminated a whole class of nuclear missiles for the first time
allowed both superpowers to build unlimited missile defences
questions.explanation: Reagan and Gorbachev agreed to destroy all ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres, with on-site inspection. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 had banned atmospheric tests.

questions.stem: Which event is often taken to mark the end of the division of Europe at the close of the Cold War?
options: the reunification of Germany in October 1990
the signing of the Helsinki Final Act in 1975
the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968
the building of the Berlin Wall in August 1961
questions.explanation: After the Berlin Wall opened in November 1989, Gorbachev accepted the reunification of Germany inside NATO, and it took place on 3 October 1990. The USSR itself was dissolved in December 1991.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains the end of the Cold War?
options: A Western invasion of Eastern Europe, the defeat of the Red Army and the occupation of Moscow by NATO forces
The victory of the Soviet Union in Afghanistan and the spread of communism to Western Europe in the 1980s
An agreement between the USA and China to divide the world into two spheres in the late 1980s
Soviet economic weakness, Gorbachev's reforms and restraint, Western pressure and popular movements in Eastern Europe
questions.explanation: Historians weigh these factors differently, but most combine long-term Soviet decline, Gorbachev's decisions not to use force, the pressure of the arms race and the people's revolutions of 1989. There was no Western invasion, and the USSR withdrew from Afghanistan.
